title: What makes an argument
body: An argument is a set of reasons offered for a conclusion. The reasons are premises. A conclusion can be interesting and still badly supported.
Ask two separate questions. Do the premises support the conclusion if they are true? Are the premises actually true? The first question is about structure. The second is about evidence.
A valid structure can still use a false premise. An invalid structure can contain true sentences and still fail to prove its conclusion. Keep the two checks apart.

title: Working memory is a workspace
body: Working memory is the small amount of information you can hold and use at the same time. It is not the same thing as long-term knowledge.

A chess calculation and a mental sum both load this workspace. When it is full, a new detail pushes an older one out. Writing a move down, or breaking a sum into parts, is a way of spending the workspace carefully.
Practice can make a particular kind of task more familiar. Familiar patterns take less space. That is a training effect, not a change in a single intelligence score.

title: A scientific claim needs a test
body: A scientific claim says something that could turn out to be false. If no observation could count against it, it is not yet a testable claim.
A fair test compares conditions that differ in the thing being studied and stay alike in the things that could confuse the result. One vivid story is not that comparison.
When you read a result, ask what was measured, what was compared, and how large the difference was. The label on the article is not the evidence.

title: Thought experiments are tools
body: A thought experiment asks you to imagine a case so that a principle becomes easier to see. It does not prove a fact about the physical world by itself.
The useful question is which assumption the case is pressing on. If two people accept the story and still reach different conclusions, name the assumption they do not share.
Treat the story as a lens, then go back to the principle in ordinary language. A memorable picture is not a substitute for the argument.

title: An example is not a proof
body: One example can show that a general claim is false. No list of examples, however long, shows that a claim about every case is true.
A proof has to cover the remaining cases, often by using the definition rather than another number. Check each step against the previous one.
When a step feels obvious, write the reason anyway. The missing reason is often the place where the argument only works for the example you had in mind.
